title: IB Theory of Knowledge may be the AI literacy course our students actually need
author: Jeff Lippman
summary: Jeff Lippman, an IB teacher, describes showing his Theory of Knowledge students a video he co-created with Claude in which the model reflects on its own existence, and the stunned, divided classroom discussion that followed. He argues that this unscripted conversation models what AI literacy should look like in high schools, going beyond how large language models work, bias and hallucination to the deeper question of what it means to understand, create and feel when machines mirror human capabilities. TOK is a natural home for this because it already asks students to examine the nature of knowledge and their own assumptions. He deliberately taught the unit on paper, with printed articles, annotation and Socratic seminars, to sustain attention and engage the ideas more deeply. Students closed the unit by choosing a question, presenting to peers and taking a position. His conclusion is that embedding AI literacy in these larger questions teaches students to keep asking questions a machine cannot answer for them.
points: Unscripted student reactions to an AI-authored self-portrait (manipulation, empathy, unease about creativity) gave the class a richer entry into AI literacy than a lesson on how models work.
Technical AI literacy (bias, hallucination, how LLMs function) is necessary but incomplete; students also need to wrestle with understanding, authorship and consciousness in an AI-immersed world.
TOK's standing questions about knowledge, such as whether a solved problem no human understands counts as knowledge, can be extended to AI without building a new course.
Studying AI through printed readings, annotation and Socratic seminar was a deliberate choice to create a tech-free space that protects attention.
A student-chosen question and peer presentation as the final assessment lets students take a position rather than merely absorb information about AI.
quotes: I had prompted the model to introduce itself in the most creative way possible, sharing its reflections on its own existence and cognition, and what that could mean to us as humans and learners.
The conversation was unscripted, uncomfortable and left many questions unresolved. But it also served as a model for what I think AI literacy should look like in our high school classrooms.
My students were wrestling with what it means to understand, create and feel in a world where AI models are mirroring human capabilities in real time.
TOK sits at the core of the IB diploma, requiring students to reflect on the very nature of knowledge itself, and become aware of their own assumptions and interpretations.

It may seem counterintuitive to study AI on paper, but the strategy was deliberate. I wanted to create a "tech-free” environment that would sustain their attention, in order to engage with the ideas more deeply.
They are not just learning about how to use AI effectively, they are also learning how to “read the world” and keep asking questions a machine can never answer for them.

The advantage my TOK students have is not that they know the answer. It is that they have already sat in the silence after that video and wrestled with the deep human consequences of our AI-immersed future.
